title: Battle of Passchendaele
description: 1917 campaign of the First World War
wiki_lead:
The Third Battle of Ypres (German: Dritte Flandernschlacht; French: Troisième Bataille des Flandres; Dutch: Derde Slag om Ieper), also known as the Battle of Passchendaele ( PASH-ən-dayl), was a campaign of the First World War, fought by the Allies against the German Empire. The battle took place on the Western Front, from July to November 1917, for control of the ridges south and east of the Belgian city of Ypres in West Flanders, as part of a strategy decided by the Entente at conferences in November 1916 and May 1917. Passchendaele (now Passendale) lies on the last ridge east of Ypres, 5 mi (8 km) from Roulers (now Roeselare), a junction of the Bruges-(Brugge)-to-Kortrijk railway. The station at Roulers was on the main supply route of the German 4th Army. Once Passchendaele Ridge had been captured, the Allied advance was to continue to a line from Thourout (now Torhout) to Couckelaere (Koekelare).
Further operations and a British supporting attack along the Belgian coast from Nieuport (Nieuwpoort), combined with an amphibious landing (Operation Hush), were to have reached Bruges and then the Dutch frontier. Although a general withdrawal had seemed inevitable in early October, the Germans were able to avoid one due to the resistance of the 4th Army, unusually wet weather in August, the beginning of the autumn rains in October and the diversion of British and French resources to Italy. The campaign ended in November, when the Canadian Corps captured Passchendaele, apart from local attacks in December and early in the new year. The Battle of the Lys (Fourth Battle of Ypres) and the Fifth Battle of Ypres of 1918, were fought before the Allies occupied the Belgian coast and reached the Dutch frontier.
A campaign in Flanders was controversial in 1917 and has remained so. The British Prime Minister, David Lloyd George, opposed the offensive, as did General Ferdinand Foch, the Chief of Staff of the French Army. Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig, commander of the British Expeditionary Force (BEF) did not receive approval for the Flanders operation from the War Cabinet until 25 July. Matters of dispute by the participants, writers and historians since 1917 include the wisdom of pursuing an offensive strategy in the wake of the Nivelle Offensive, rather than waiting for the arrival of the American Expeditionary Force (AEF) in France.
Controversies also debated are the choice of Flanders, its climate, the selection of General Hubert Gough and the Fifth Army to conduct the offensive and debates over the nature of the opening attack and between advocates of shallow and deeper objectives. Also debated are the time between the Battle of Messines (7–14 June) and the first Allied attack (the Battle of Pilckem Ridge, 31 July) the extent to which the French Army mutinies influenced the British, the effect of the exceptional weather, the decision to continue the offensive in October and the human costs of the campaign.

grok_lead: The Battle of Passchendaele, also known as the Third Battle of Ypres, was a prolonged British-led offensive against entrenched German positions in the Flanders region near Ypres, Belgium, from 31 July to 10 November 1917 during the First World War. Commanded by Field Marshal Sir Douglas Haig, the campaign sought to exploit German diversions from the Russian front and French mutinies by advancing toward the Belgian coast to disrupt U-boat operations and potentially outflank German lines. Involving primarily British Expeditionary Force units augmented by Australian, New Zealand, Canadian, and South African Dominion troops, with initial French cooperation, it pitted around 50 Allied divisions against the German Fourth Army under General Friedrich Sixt von Armin. Unusually heavy rainfall throughout the offensive turned the reclaimed polder landscape into a deep, clinging mud that drowned men, horses, and equipment, while destroying drainage systems and rendering shell-cratered ground nearly impassable, which compounded the challenges of massed artillery barrages and infantry assaults across barbed wire and concrete pillboxes. Despite early successes like the capture of Pilckem Ridge and later limited gains at Broodseinde, the operation stalled amid mounting losses, culminating in Canadian Corps assaults that seized Passchendaele ridge and village at the cost of over 15,000 casualties in the final phase alone. The battle resulted in approximately 275,000 British Empire casualties and 220,000 to 270,000 German losses for an advance of barely five miles, yielding no strategic breakthrough and exposing the limitations of attrition warfare under Haig's persistent direction despite deteriorating weather and intelligence indicating German reinforcements. It remains a emblematic case of industrialized slaughter on the Western Front, where tactical innovations like creeping barrages proved insufficient against environmental catastrophe and defensive depth, fueling postwar critiques of high command optimism over empirical battlefield realities.
